Similar to Tract III, ground-water discharge from the reclaimed aquifer on Tract II should correspond to the contact between the reclaimed aquifer and the top of the sub-Robinson unit, with essentially no discharge from interior shallow drainageways.
There should not be substantial effect on the springs discharging from the sub-Robinson rocks along Tracts II and III after reclamation is complete and equilibrium condition have been re-established. There may be a decrease in the discharge of these springs because of a probable decrease in the vertical head gradient between the overlying material and the sub-Robinson materials.
After mining, the total discharge from springs around and on both tracts may be slightly higher due to increased rates of infiltration and permeability of the reclaimed aquifer. This effect will probably be concentrated in springs currently originating from the Robinson Coal. It is expected that flows from some springs will be somewhat greater in the winter and spring and less in the summer because of the characteristics of the reclaimed aquifer.
Hydrogeologic aspects similar to those at Tract III occur at the existing Decker surface coal mine in southeastern Montana. Mining at the Decker mine has been in progress since 1972. During the mining operation water levels in observation wells have declined according to their relative distance from the mine and according to the wells position relative to the mine and recharge direction (Van Voast and Hedges, 1975 a). Water levels declined more than 10 feet within 1 1/2 miles of the active mine but water-level declines have been much less extensive on the recharge side of the mine.
